content: This is an updated review of the efficacy and tolerability of lacosamide as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy, building upon the Cochrane review published in 2015. Approximately 50% of individuals with epilepsy do not achieve seizure freedom with their first antiepileptic drug, and about one-third fail to achieve complete seizure control despite trying multiple antiepileptic medications. Lacosamide has been approved as an adjunctive treatment for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and tolerability of lacosamide as an add-on therapy in both children and adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies, MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, was conducted up to August 22, 2019. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating lacosamide as an adjunctive treatment in this population were included. The outcomes assessed included a ≥50% reduction in seizure frequency, seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal, adverse events, quality of life, and cognitive changes. Standard Cochrane methodology was employed, and subgroup analyses were performed based on lacosamide dose and patient age. Five RCTs involving 2,199 participants were included in the analysis. All studies were placebo-controlled, double-blind, and evaluated lacosamide doses ranging from 200 mg to 600 mg per day. One study included children, while the others focused on adults. The trial durations ranged from 24 to 26 weeks. The risk of bias across the studies was judged to be low to unclear, and the overall certainty of evidence was rated as moderate to high, except for seizure freedom, which was rated as low-certainty evidence. The results showed that lacosamide significantly increased the likelihood of achieving a ≥50% reduction in seizure frequency compared to placebo, with a risk ratio (RR) of 1.79 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.55 to 2.08; high-certainty evidence). The RR for seizure freedom was 2.27 (95% CI 1.35 to 3.83; low-certainty evidence). The RR for treatment withdrawal due to any cause was 1.57 (95% CI 1.24 to 1.98; moderate-certainty evidence). Sensitivity analyses revealed that the exclusion of pediatric data nearly doubled the RR for seizure freedom (RR 4.04, 95% CI 1.52 to 10.73). Adverse events associated with lacosamide included abnormal coordination (RR 6.12, 99% CI 1.35 to 27.77), blurred vision (RR 4.65, 99% CI 1.24 to 17.37), diplopia (RR 5.59, 99% CI 2.27 to 13.79), dizziness (RR 2.96, 99% CI 2.09 to 4.20), nausea (RR 2.35, 99% CI 1.37 to 4.02), somnolence (RR 2.04, 99% CI 1.22 to 3.41), vomiting (RR 2.94, 99% CI 1.54 to 5.64), and experiencing one or more adverse events (RR 1.12, 99% CI 1.01 to 1.24). Adverse events that were not statistically significant included vertigo, rash, nasopharyngitis, headache, fatigue, nystagmus, and upper respiratory tract infections. In conclusion, lacosamide is effective and well-tolerated in the short term as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. It increases the likelihood of achieving a ≥50% reduction in seizure frequency and may improve seizure freedom compared to placebo. However, higher doses of lacosamide are associated with increased rates of adverse events and treatment withdrawal. Further research is needed to evaluate its use in children and to assess its long-term efficacy and tolerability.
